{
  "jobspec": "#!/bin/bash
# Flux batch script converted from Slurm

# NOTE: Run with: flux batch <this_script>

# Slurm resources:
#   --time=20-01:00:00
#   --ntasks=1
#   --cpus-per-task=20
#   --mem-per-cpu=7500
#   --partition=bio

#flux: -n 1
#flux: -c 20
#flux: --time-limit=481h

# Omitted Slurm option: --mem-per-cpu=7500
# Flux memory requests are site/config dependent and not universally portable.
# Performance implication: job may be scheduled on nodes with insufficient memory, risking OOM kills or degraded performance.

# Omitted Slurm option: --partition=bio
# Flux queues/partitions are site-specific; no portable equivalent.
# Performance implication: job may run on different hardware or have different priority/limits (or be rejected by policy).

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=20
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=20

module --ignore-cache load Nextflow/21.08.0

nextflow run Braker.nf --genome=<genome.fna> --prot=<BrakerDB> --SRA=none --brakermode=<mode> --cpu=20 --currentpath=<PWD>
"
}

export MKL_NUM_THREADS=20

module --ignore-cache load Nextflow/21.08.0

nextflow run Braker.nf --genome=<genome.fna> --prot=<BrakerDB> --SRA=none --brakermode=<mode> --cpu=20 --currentpath=<PWD>

reasons: The original Slurm job requested memory per CPU (`--mem-per-cpu=7500`) but the Flux resource section has no memory request; on systems that schedule/enforce memory this can under-provision the job and risk OOM or degraded performance.

The original Slurm job targeted a specific partition (`--partition=bio`) but the Flux resource section has no queue/partition constraint; this can change scheduling eligibility and allocated hardware.
